Furthermore, they are equally convinced, that their field of choice was the right one; and from their own perspective each one of them was right. Since you're HN, you might have a particular interest towards this field we call "business". Now, this is not what people around you -who are called "managers" btw- do. comments.text_zh: 如果你想找点不一样的东西，可以看看 Randy Pausch 的 The Last Lecture。从一种非常反传统意义上说，这是一本让人大开眼界的书。你可能还记得 Pausch，他是 Carnegie Mellon 的计算机科学教授，曾被医生告知自己只剩几个月的生命（癌症）。这本书没有偏离它的主题：“如果我们知道自己只剩最后一次机会，我们会向世界传授什么智慧？”如果你在寻找动力，以及一种“跳出框架”来分析日常生活的方式，那就是它了。书在这里：[LINK] 著名演讲在这里：[VIDEO]
comments.text: If you're looking for something different then check out The Last Lecture by Randy Pausch. It's is an eye-opening book in a very nontraditional sense. You may remember Pausch as the computer science professor at Carnegie Mellon who was told that he had but a few months left to live (cancer). This book doesn't stray from its topic: "What wisdom would we impart to the world if we knew it was our last chance?" If you're looking for motivation and an "out of the box" approach to analyzing daily life then this is it. Here's the book: [LINK] Here's the famous speech: [VIDEO]

comments.text_zh: 这让我想起 Randy Pausch 让别人坐下来一起吃午饭的方法。[1] “然后他问了一个问题。我当时想，抱歉，你是说你叫 Tom Furness 吗？他说是。我说，那我很乐意回答你的问题，但首先，你明天愿意和我一起吃午饭吗？那个小小的瞬间里有很多东西。有很多谦逊，但同时也是在一个对方几乎不可能拒绝的情境下向他提出请求。”不过得承认，那是在你已经让对方跟你说了几句话、而且你正站在一大群人面前之后。[1] [VIDEO] 19:40 编辑：给不知道的人补充一下这场演讲的背景：这场演讲是 CMU 举办的“Last Lecture”系列之一，假设情境是“如果你只能做最后一场演讲，你会讲什么？”。CMU 教授 Randy Pausch 并不需要假装。他被诊断出胰腺癌，而在 2007 年 8 月（他做这场演讲时）被告知只剩三到六个月的生命。如果你还没看过，就把整场演讲看了吧。真的很好。
comments.text: This reminds me of Randy Pausch's method of getting someone to sit down for lunch. [1] "And he asked a question. And I was like, I’m sorry did you say you were Tom Furness? And he said yes. I said, then I would love to answer your question, but first, will you have lunch with me tomorrow? And there’s a lot in that little moment. There’s a lot of humility, but also asking a person where he can’t possibly say no." Although, admittedly, that's after you got them to say a few words to you and you're in front of a large group of people. [1] [VIDEO] 19:40 Edit: For those who don't know, here's the setting of this talk: This talk is one in a series given at CMU called the "Last Lecture" series with the hypothetical setting of 'what if you had one last talk to give?'. Randy Pausch, a professor at CMU, didn't have to pretend. He was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer, and in August of 2007 (when he gave the talk) was told he had three to six months left to live. If you haven't seen it, watch the whole talk. It's really good.

comments.story_title: I’m 22 and I’ve failed
comments.why_zh: 推荐给一个觉得自己失败的年轻人。
comments.quote_zh: 帮自己一个忙，花点时间看看这个演讲
comments.text_zh: 哦，天哪！人生是马拉松，不是短跑。你还年轻（等你到 32 岁、42 岁、52 岁时再回想这句话）。所以，听我说。你需要培养习惯，赢的习惯，每次都赢，建立一套学习和改进的流程，并且相信这个流程。无视失败，在有些人眼里你可能显得无趣又不成功，但一旦你的习惯开始起作用，它就能改变你的轨道。孩子，你没有失败。你是在成长，生活就是这样。如果你读过很多书/传记，你会发现一些非常成功的人也曾经历挫折。无视那些消极沮丧的低语，去学习，多读书。我们大多数人以前都处在那样的境地，帮自己一个忙，花点时间看看这个演讲《最后一课：实现你童年的梦想》，Randy Pausch [VIDEO]
comments.text: Oh Boy! Life is a marathon, not a sprint. You are still young (revisit these words when you reach 32, 42, and 52). So, hear me out. You need to work on developing habits, habits of winning, winning every time, develop a process of learning and improving and trust the process. Ignore failures, you might look boring and unsuccessful to some people, but once your habits start to work, it can change your orbit. You’re not failing, boy. You are growing up and this is how life look like. If you read a lot of books/biographies, you will realize how some very successful people have had setbacks. Ignore these negative depressing whispers, and learn, read more. Most of us were in that spot before, do yourself a favor, and take some time to watch this talk "Last Lecture: Achieving Your Childhood Dreams", Randy Pausch [VIDEO]

comments.text_zh: 已故的 Dr. Randy Pausch，因 Last Lecture 而闻名，曾说他的原则是归档所有邮件，没有例外。[1] 如果我没记错，这是因为他认为，如果每个人都保存所有邮件，就会为未来的历史学家提供一座同时代研究资料的宝库。从法律角度看，清除邮件可能会招致“证据销毁”（spoliation of evidence）的指控，[2] 在某些情况下，这可能导致法官指示陪审团，陪审员可以推定你销毁的内容对你的案件不利。你可以辩称自己没有清除任何相关邮件，但这会变成各执一词的问题。[1] 我相信这出现在他 [VIDEO] 的 Last Lecture 中，但也可能是在他 [LINK] 的时间管理讲座里 [2] [LINK]
comments.text: The late Dr. Randy Pausch, of Last Lecture fame, said that his rule was to archive all emails, no exceptions. [1] IIRC it was because he figured that if everyone saved all their emails, it would would provide future historians with a treasure trove of contemporaneous research material. From a legal perspective, purging emails can lead to accusations of "spoliation of evidence," [2] which in some circumstances can lead to the judge instructing the jury that the jurors can presume that what you destroyed was harmful to your case. You can argue that you didn't purge any relevant emails, but that becomes a he-said/she-said issue. [1] I believe it was in his Last Lecture at [VIDEO] , but it might have been his time-management lecture at [LINK] [2] [LINK]

comments.text_zh: 已故的 Randy Pausch 在 Carnegie Mellon 大学的 Last Lecture[1] 中给出了……嗯，很多很好的建议，但跳进我脑海里的那一段是：“知道自己什么时候身处于一场撒尿比赛中，这非常重要。而尽快从中脱身，也非常重要。”这件事看起来极像一场撒尿比赛，而且对手不只是 Hollywood 的那一位房主——而是每一个有同样感受的人。我敢打赌，这个集合的基数可不是个小数目。它到底是不是一场撒尿比赛并不重要。它看起来像。如果我掌管着这个州，我宁愿把时间和精力花在真正能 Get People To Wear Masks 的事情上，而不是再来一轮 Pissing Match: San Andreas。[1] [VIDEO]
comments.text: The late Randy Pausch, in his Last Lecture[1] at Carnegie Mellon University, offered up... well, a lot of great advice, but the piece that jumped into my mind was: "It’s very important to know when you’re in a pissing match. And it’s very important to get out of it as quickly as possible." This thing looks awfully like a pissing match, and it's not just with the one homeowner in Hollywood -- it's with every person that feels the same way. I would lay good money the cardinality of that set is not a small number. Doesn't matter whether or not it is a pissing match. It looks like one. Were I running the state, I'd rather spend my time and energy on doing things that would actually Get People To Wear Masks, as opposed to another round of Pissing Match: San Andreas. [1] [VIDEO]
